1: Chapter 1: A Visitor in the Rain
It had been raining on Pierrefeu for three days. That spring, Claire Martin’s older sister had left for Paris, and since then Claire had been running the village’s small pharmacy alone.
At nightfall, she closed the shutters, counted the day’s receipts, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had barely lain down when someone hammered furiously at the door downstairs. A man’s voice called, “Is anyone there?”
A young man stood on the threshold, soaked to the skin, his left arm clutched in bloodstained cloth. He introduced himself: his name was Pierre Lapin, and he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
“I need treatment,” Lapin said quietly. “I can pay. Three thousand five hundred francs—will that be enough?”
He took a letter wrapped in oilcloth from his coat. “This letter must reach the abbey at Saint-Vent before May 18.”
Since her sister had left, Claire often felt low in the evenings, but that night she had no time to dwell on it.
Yet she refused his money and said only, “At dawn tomorrow, I will take you into the mountains.”
2: At daybreak, they set off. Claire carried a basket on her back containing bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

Halfway up the slope, they met old Gaston Roux, who was chopping wood. He set down his axe and told them in a low voice that, the previous evening, three strangers had questioned people at the village entrance about a wounded young man.
“Take the footpath, my little Claire,” Gaston Roux said. “The main road isn’t safe.” Claire thanked him.
The path was narrow and slippery. Claire walked ahead, placing each foot with confidence. Lapin followed her without a word.
At noon, the rain stopped; the mist slowly lifted, and the roof of the Saint-Vent abbey appeared in the distance. A nun, Sister Agnès, stood before the door, responsible for welcoming visitors.
Sister Agnès took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. “The abbess has been waiting for this letter for 2 years.”
Lapin said to Claire, “I owe you my life.” Claire smiled. “Then next time, fix the roof of my pharmacy.” Lapin stayed at the abbey.
That evening, Claire walked back down the mountain alone. When she reached home, it was already dark; she lit the lamp and sat for a long time behind the counter.
